newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Shell's Wavin to expand in Eastern Europe.
newsitem.headline: Shell's Wavin to expand in Eastern Europe.

text.p: Unlisted Dutch plastics maker Wavin BV said it expected further growth in years ahead with Eastern Europe as one of its focus areas for expansion.

"Central and eastern Europe remains an attractive area for us," chairman Fons Driessen told a news conference. He said Wavin was now active in seven countries in the region but wanted to be present in more.
Wavin, which is 50 percent owned by Royal Dutch/Shell, is also in talks about takeovers in France and the Netherlands, but these are not expected to be finalised until the second half of this year.

Outside of Europe, Wavin is seeking growth in Southeast Asia and at a later stage in Latin America. It will probably start here by taking minority stakes in firms with the option to increase these to majority interests.
Wavin has just started to reassess its group structure with consultants McKinsey in order to identify its most profitable geographic areas and realise further cost cuts.
The company plans to raise its turnover, which totalled 1.64 billion guilders in 1996, to about two billion in the year 2000 and to more than three billion in 2005, Driessen said.
In 2005, Wavin aims at a return on its shareholders' equity of about 15 percent, compared with 10.5 percent in 1996.
Earlier, it said it expected the 1997 net profit to be slightly higher than 1996's 37 million guilders.

The long-term process of concentrating on the core activity of plastic pipes and pipe systems will be concluded this year by the previously announced sale of two units which produce industrial foils and recycled foils.
After these sales, Wavin will have divested 11 units of its foils, garbage bags and crates division over the period 1991-1997, with total sales of about 500 million guilders.
Last year's turnover was not only depressed by the sale of some subsidiaries but also by the recession in the German construction sector and volatile raw materials prices.

Driessen said he did not expect a recovery in Germany to emerge for the next two or three years. Wavin's German units were now operating at break-even level but many competitors had suffered substantial losses there, he added.
Southern Europe also remained a problem area and Driessen said the Spanish plant near the city of Bilbao would be "thoroughly reorganised" this year.
"The losses there (in Spain) are too big to carry them with us," Driessen said. He added the Bilbao plant suffered annual losses of several million guilders but declined to elaborate.
Wavin has held talks with various parties about selling the Spanish plant, but the bad market situation there has prevented a successful sale.
Driessen said he could not yet give more details about possible job cuts at the Spanish production site, which currently employs about 100 people.
